newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Cattle cloning seen at commercial doorstep.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Cattle cloning seen at commercial doorstep.

text.p: The reported cloning of more than 400 cattle by Australian scientists puts the process on the doorstep of commercial production, Australian scientists said.
The production of a large number of clones from a single embryo was the first time cloning had been achieved anywhere in the world on such a scale, they said.

Alan Trounson of Monash University, Melbourne, and Bernie Harford of Genetics Australia, who are reported to have created more than 400 cattle clones from a single embryo, were not available for comment on Thursday.
Trounson and Harford were reported by New Scientist magazine on Thursday as having created 470 cattle clones from embryos and as wanting to create a reliable herd of prize cattle.
Other Australian scientists had reservations about the full extent of the achievement and about whether food products from clones would find acceptance in sensitive consumer markets.

Traders who sell Australian beef and other foodstuffs into Asia and elsewhere on Thursday also pondered whether cloned meat would sell in countries where consumers were particular about the source of their food.

"This is a terrific technical achievement, an order of magnitude (achieved) more than anybody else. (But) it's a production process, not a research process," Oliver Mayo, chief of the animal production division of Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), said.
"It is of commercial significance today," he said.

But Mayo and other Australian scientists, most from the transgenics school which seeks to breed super-products rather than make clone copies of existing animals, said Trounson's breakthrough was limited.
"This is what looks like a production tool, rather than a research tool," Mayo said.

Professor Laurie Piper of the Cooperative Research Centre for Premium Quality Wool, who is working to produce a Australian transgenic wool, said the cloning process was limited by a need to copy an existing animal.
Cloning techniques had low success rates and were very costly, he said.
"Embryonic cloning is widespread around the world. I don't think there's anything much new in that at all," Piper added.
Trounson's 400-clone volume breakthrough follows the cloning of a sheep by Scottish scientist Ian Wilmut, who introduced cloned Dolly to the world last month, sparking major debate.
Mayo believes that Trounson's real breakthrough will be to make possible the mass production of hundreds of Dolly-type clones at a time.
"I'd say what (Trounson's) really doing is saying 'here we are - we can do it for you'," Mayo said.
Mayo and other Australian transgenicists go a step further to say the Trounson breakthrough may allow clone-production of hundreds of transgenically-produced animals.
A major problem with Trounson's approach was that it produced multiple identical animals at the top of the breeding pyramid, which would inevitably produce in-breeding, Mayo said.
"If they're all identical you've got to be very careful who you mate them with and who you mate their daughters with."

But combination of the Trounson breakthrough with transgenics and proven adult cloning methods opened the potential for accelerated advance. "Perhaps animal breeders can catch up a bit with plant breeders," he said.

Leading executives from Japanese trading house Mitsui and Co (Australia) on Thursday pondered whether Asian markets would accept cloned meat. They were fascinated by the Trounson advance but without quick views on the likely meat market response.
Scientists such as Mayo see a definite resistance problem.

"It's very natural to worry about extreme cases of things," he said. "People will accept quite grotesque levels of risk if they inflict them on themselves, but they won't accept quite absurdly low risks if they come from somebody else."
"The flavour-saver tomato on the market has stirred people up. That has a gene from a flatfish. People feel that's against nature," he said.
"(But) so is a bulldog for goodness sake," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
